problem:
Consider the matrices

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,E=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

- $CD=DC={I}_{3}$
- $CE=EC={I}_{3}$
- $D={C}^{-1}$

feedback.worked_solution:
We'll work out the indefinite integral first and then proceed with the definite integral.

First, we note that a denominator of the integrand can be factored as

$$
{x}^{2}-2x-8=(x+2)(x-4).
$$

So the integrand can be converted into a sum of partial fractions,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3x-6}{{x}^{2}-2x-8} & =\frac{3x-6}{(x+2)(x-4)}=\frac{A}{x+2}+\frac{B}{x-4},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
3x-6=A(x-4)+B(x+2).
$$

Plugging in $x=4,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3(4)-6 & =A(4-4)+B(4+2) \\ 6 & =6B \\ B & =1\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=-2,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3(-2)-6 & =A(-2-4)+B(-2+2) \\ -12 & =-6A \\ A & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{3x-6}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}=\frac{2}{x+2}+\frac{1}{x-4}.
$$

Now, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3x-6}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{2}{x+2}+\frac{1}{x-4})\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{x+2}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{x-4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+2|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3x-6}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}\,\text{d}x & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+2|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x+2)^{2}|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x+2)^{2}(x-4)|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the definite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{3}\frac{3x-6}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x+2)^{2}(x-4)|{|}_{-1}^{3} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡5 \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡5-\operatorname{ln}⁡5 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡5.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Find the inverse of the following matrix:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 6 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
Notice that we're given a Frobenius matrix:

- all entries on the main diagonal are ones

- the matrix has only one column (the $1$st column) where some entries below the main diagonal are not zeros

- all the other entries outside the main diagonal are zeros

To find the inverse of a Frobenius matrix, we simply take the non-zero entries outside the main diagonal with opposite signs. 

In our case, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 6 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -6 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that ${E}_{1}$ and ${E}_{2}$ are both elementary matrices.

First, we need to find ${E}_{1}^{-1}.$ We write down ${E}_{1}$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[{E}_{1}\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 8 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-8){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{E}_{1}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -8 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we can find the product ${E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}:$

$$
{E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -8 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -6 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}49 & -8 \\ -6 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$
